chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Harun ibn al-Jahm, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

When the women emigrated to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), a woman among them named Umm Habeeb emigrated, and she was a circumciser who would circumcise the girls. When the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) saw her, he said to her: 'O Umm Habeeb, the work that was in your hand is in your hand today.' She said, 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah, except if it is forbidden, so forbid me from it.' He said, 'No, but it is permissible. So come closer to me until I teach you.' She said, 'So I came closer to him, and he said: O Umm Habeeb, when you do it, do not overdo it, i.e., do not amputate it completely, and snip it, for it is brighter for the face and more pleasing to the husband.'
ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on female circumcision according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Kafi clarifies the nature of female circumcision (khitan al-jawari) as a moderate practice rather than a complete excision, with the Prophet advising Umm Habeeb to 'snip' (ashmi) rather than 'uproot' (la tanhaki) to preserve beauty and marital harmony. In Shia scholarship, this is often cited to support the recommendation (mustahabb) of a light, non-damaging procedure, distinguishing it from the more extensive forms practiced in other traditions. The narration highlights the practical wisdom of maintaining physical integrity while enhancing aesthetic and conjugal pleasure.
